e: The most recent 2 years must stay highly available and immediately retrievable, so keep them in S3 Standard, then move to Glacier Deep Archive after 2 years for the lowest-cost long-term retention (25 years). Immediate transition or One Zone-IA would break the availability or retrieval requirement.

EC2 instance store provides the highest I/O performance for temporary processing, S3 is highly durable for 300 TB of media, and S3 Glacier is the cheap choice for 900 TB of archive. EFS is much more expensive at this size and EBS can't give the same maximum I/O or durability profile as S3 for this volume.

Stateless containers that tolerate interruptions suit Spot Instances for the lowest cost, and an EKS managed node group handles node provisioning and lifecycle, reducing operational work. Self-managed Auto Scaling groups require more management, and On-Demand costs more.

Aurora PostgreSQL gives a managed, scalable database without infrastructure upkeep, and ECS on Fargate runs the existing containers without managing servers or capacity. EC2 hosting keeps the operational burden, and CloudFront or ElastiCache don't address infrastructure maintenance.

A target tracking scaling policy automatically adds or removes instances to keep a metric, such as average CPU, at a target like 40%. Simple scaling and scheduled scaling are less precise, and a custom Lambda function adds unnecessary work.

An origin access identity (OAI) lets CloudFront access the S3 bucket, and the bucket permissions allow only the OAI to read objects, so direct S3 URLs are blocked. (Origin access control is the newer equivalent.) IAM users can't be assigned to CloudFront, and a distribution ID isn't a bucket policy principal in this older design.

S3 stores the downloadable reports, and CloudFront caches them at edge locations worldwide for the fastest response, scaling automatically with no servers to provision. Lambda with DynamoDB, or EC2 and load balancers, would require more provisioning and cost.

RDS Custom for Oracle gives a managed database with access to the underlying operating system, which standard RDS doesn't allow, and a cross-Region read replica provides DR with low overhead. EC2 requires heavy self-management, and standard RDS blocks OS access.

Athena runs SQL serverlessly directly on S3 data, S3 CRR replicates encrypted objects to another Region, and SSE-KMS with multi-Region keys works across both Regions. RDS isn't serverless querying of S3, and SSE-S3 doesn't give the key control needed for the replicated data.

With AWS PrivateLink, the provider exposes the service through a VPC endpoint service, and the company creates an interface endpoint in its VPC. Connectivity is private, limited to the target service, and initiated only from the consumer side. VPC peering exposes whole networks, and a NAT gateway uses the internet.

AWS DMS needs a replication instance (server) and an ongoing replication task (change data capture) to keep Aurora synchronized while the source stays online. SCT isn't needed for same-engine PostgreSQL migration, and a backup alone doesn't keep systems in sync.

Using distribution lists as root email addresses that reach a few administrators avoids a single person missing notices and keeps notifications limited to admins, and alternate contacts can be configured for billing, operations, and security. Forwarding to everyone or a single person is unsafe, and using the same root email on all accounts isn't allowed.

Amazon MQ active/standby for RabbitMQ is managed and highly available across AZs, a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group keeps the application available, and RDS for PostgreSQL Multi-AZ removes database management. Self-managed RabbitMQ or PostgreSQL on EC2 in Auto Scaling groups adds operational overhead.

S3 replication automatically copies new files to the analysis bucket with no code, and EventBridge notifications can trigger both Lambda and SageMaker Pipelines as targets (S3 event notifications can't target SageMaker Pipelines directly). This is the least operational overhead.

Interruptible, unpredictable EC2 ingestion fits Spot Instances at the lowest cost. A Compute Savings Plan covers predictable Fargate and Lambda usage, since it applies to EC2, Fargate, and Lambda (EC2 instance Savings Plans do not cover Fargate or Lambda). Reserved Instances don't suit sporadic usage.

CloudFront with the ALB as an origin accelerates both static and dynamic content over the AWS global network and edge locations (including TLS termination near users). Serving dynamic content directly from the ALB, or using Route 53 routing alone, gives higher latency for distant users.

Global Accelerator supports UDP, provides static anycast IP addresses, and routes users to the nearest edge location over the AWS backbone. An NLB handles UDP to EC2 instances running the custom kernel application. CloudFront, API Gateway, and ALBs don't support UDP, and Lambda can't run a modified kernel.

Containers on ECS let the company keep most of the existing code, split the monolith into smaller services owned by different teams, and scale with low operational overhead behind an ALB. Lambda or Amplify would require rewriting a lot of code, and EC2 means more management.

Running reports against an Aurora Replica (reader endpoint) removes the read load from the primary instance, at the cost of just a replica. Redshift migration is more work, and a larger instance or more IOPS costs more without isolating the reporting load.

Moving the database to Aurora, then putting the web tier in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB with a Spot Fleet, scales seamlessly and keeps costs low. Two fixed On-Demand instances don't scale automatically, and stopping the instance to resize causes downtime.

Reserved Instances cover the steady baseline at a discount, and Spot Instances handle the extra peak capacity cheaply, and since the app is stateless the interruptions are acceptable without hurting availability. Spot for everything risks availability, and On-Demand or Dedicated Instances cost more.

S3 lifecycle policies can automatically move logs older than a month to Glacier Deep Archive, the cheapest storage for 10-year retention. AWS Backup doesn't tier S3 data this way, and CloudWatch Logs is more expensive for storing 10 TB per month.

Configuring an SQS queue as the Lambda on-failure destination captures failed events so they aren't lost, and the function can process them later until all notifications are eventually handled. Multiple AZs and more memory don't address failures, and SNS retry settings alone have limits.
An SQS FIFO queue preserves the order of messages, and Lambda can process them with little operational effort. Standard queues and SNS don't guarantee ordering.

CloudWatch composite alarms combine multiple alarms with AND/OR logic, so an alert fires only when CPU is above 50% and read IOPS is high together, which reduces false alarms. Dashboards don't alert, canaries monitor endpoints, and a single metric alarm can't combine multiple metrics.
